en: The Epistle of Pure Jewels (Vimalaratnalekha)
In the language of India: *Vimalaratnalekha*. In the language of Tibet: *Dri ma med pa rin po che’i phrin yig ces bya ba*.
Homage to the Guru!
Salutation to the goddess Tārā.
Having seen the body of Mahāgati, he caused the teaching of the Buddha to flourish; protecting the kingdom according to the Dharma, King Nayapāla came to power. || 1 ||
"O King, because you previously practiced giving, the ten wholesome actions, the poṣadha vows, patience, and vigor, you have now attained perfection. (2)

(2) Receive with devotion and upon your head this command of the gurus, consisting of the Sūtras and other teachings that follow the Dharma; it will be for the benefit of both yourself and others. || 3 ||
Abandoning all doubt, exert great effort for the sake of accomplishment;
avoiding drowsiness and lethargy, one should always apply oneself with vigor.
(3) By means of mindfulness, knowledge, and vigilance, one should always guard the doors of the senses;
furthermore, day and night, one should repeatedly examine the continuum of the mind. || 5 ||
One should perceive one's own faults as with eyes open, but perceive the faults of others as if blind;
one should always cultivate mindfulness, non-egoism, and emptiness. (6)
(4) One should proclaim one's own faults and not pursue the delusions of another;
one should proclaim the virtues of another but conceal one's own virtues. 7.
One should abandon gain and honor, and always renounce self-exaltation;
one should cultivate loving-kindness and compassion, and make the mind of awakening firm.
(5) The ten unwholesome actions are to be abandoned; faith must always be made firm.
One should remember even a slight sense of endearment, contentment, and compassion for those who have acted [kindly]. 9.
Anger and pride must be abandoned, and a humble state of mind should be cultivated;
wrong livelihood must be avoided, and one should live by a life of righteousness. 10.
(6) One should avoid all worldly gain and, through the wealth of the Noble Ones, make oneself perfected.
One should always abandon social assembly and dwell in the forest. || 11 ||
One should abandon incoherent speech and always remain pure and self-restrained;
upon seeing one's guru or preceptor, one should perform service with faith.
One should generate the perception of the Teacher toward distinguished persons who possess the eye of Dharma, as well as toward individuals who are beginners in their practice. || 13 ||
Upon seeing all sentient beings tormented by suffering, one should generate the thought of awakening and conceive of them as one's mother, father, and child. (14)
Abandoning all worldly activities, constantly cultivate meditative absorption;
shun evil friends and rely upon virtuous friends. 15.
(8) Upon seeing monks who are immoral, others who are devoid of the Dharma, and those of evil conduct, he shall not desist from subduing them. 16.
By all those who lack virtuous friends, by all those who associate with evildoers, and by those devoid of faith in the Three Jewels, in their gurus, preceptors, and teachers. || 17 ||
(9) One should not dwell [with those] who are ungrateful, whose intellects are concerned only with this world, and who have little faith in the next life, once three days have passed. 18.
Having abandoned the wicked and inauspicious ground, one should go where there is auspiciousness;
that which is characterized by passion should be relinquished, and one should dwell without attachment.
For attachment, failing to lead one to a happy rebirth, severs the life-force of liberation;
therefore, one should dwell constantly wherever a spiritual friend resides. 20.
(10) Always relying upon the guru, one should constantly study the collection of sūtras.
Whatever was first undertaken at the beginning, that alone should be accomplished;
otherwise, neither will succeed. || 21 ||
One should strive for the confession of sins toward others and for supreme merit;
one should always protect the world by conforming to proper conduct and maintain a mind directed toward the next world. (22)
(11) When the mind becomes uplifted, one should cut off pride;
in the absence of heedfulness, the teacher’s instruction must be remembered. || 23 ||
When a sunken mind arises, one should even praise mental uplift;
by recollecting the Perfection of Wisdom, one should bring all conceptual proliferation to rest. (24)
(12) When an object of passion or hatred arises, one should view it as being like an illusory manifestation;
upon hearing words of censure, one should understand them to be like an echo. || 25 ||
(13) When bodily affliction arises, one should contemplate past karma,
dwelling in remote forests like a dead deer.
Where one is not known by anyone, there one should conceal oneself from oneself;
one should rely upon one's chosen deity in the presence of desire, malice, torpor, and lethargy. (27)
When the mind gives rise to laziness or drowsiness, then one should enumerate one's own sins;
one should remember one's vows in the heart and contemplate impermanence and death. (28)
When standing before another, one should speak calmly and straightforwardly.
One must abandon laughter with a frowning face;
one should always remain smiling and constantly cultivate affection for others. (29)
(14) Through freedom from stinginess, one should take delight in renunciation;
envy must always be abandoned;
and one should protect the minds of others.
All doctrines are to be abandoned. || 30 ||
One should not form new attachments without prior familiarity;
one should always be proficient in mantra;
and, being always patient and having few desires, one should practice contentment. || 31 ||
(15) One should possess the consciousness of being a servant of a *caṇḍāla* regarding shamelessness (*apatrapā*) when there is knowledge of shame (*lajjā*).
One should strive for that [shame] which accomplishes the welfare of the next world, and one should exercise self-restraint. 32.
One should abandon contempt for others and abide in faith and virtue;
when giving instruction to others, one should act with a mind of compassion and a desire to help. || 33 ||
(16) One should never abandon faith in the Buddha’s Dharma nor the True Dharma;
one should always maintain faith in the Three Jewels and purify the three realms of saṃsāra. || 34 ||
Having first approached with compassion three times during the day and night, one should undertake the three aggregates of the well-known sevenfold service. (35)
One who desires to eliminate the suffering of the world should establish a noble vow;
one should desire the maturation of sentient beings and awakening, and should dedicate everything toward great awakening. || 36 ||
(17) Having made a vow, one should be constantly diligent.
When this is done, the two goals are accomplished and the two obscurations are exhausted. || 37 ||
The attainment of a human body becomes meaningful;
one attains nirvāṇa in this very life;
and the welfare of both oneself and others is accomplished.
And the supreme reality is attained. || 38 ||

(18) "The young cuckoo of the summer season warbles sweetly"—does the young peacock not also warble sweetly? Although this has been said by many scholars, it is nevertheless written here for the purpose of severing the vices of kings. 39.
Speak this discourse with the intention of promoting the highest good; speak it also to other wise people. (19) Constantly remember the six deities and practice the pure vow.
O King, protect [your subjects] according to dharma and practice self-restraint. || 40 ||
The complete forty verses entitled *Vimalaratnalekha*, sent from the elder and great scholar Dīpaṅkaraśrījñāna to King Nayapāla, are finished.
At that very time, forty verses were exchanged by that same teacher, the monk Parivarttaka, and Jayaśīla. (20)
